catalog_quote: Cemuhi is of particular interest in being one of the very few Oceanic languages with phonemic tone. This sketch is based on Rivierre (1980). ... Cemuhi also distinguishes three register tones: high, mid and low. Contrast is illustrated in the following minimal triplet: /te:/ [high tone] 'heavy' /te:/ [mid tone] 'run against, jostle' /te:/ [low tone] 'to fly' A number of grammatical morphemes have what Rivierre calls a 'neutral' tone: the tone harmonises with that of the preceding syllable. ... Perhaps 95% of words are isotonal, with only a single specification for tone needed for the whole word. However, the remaining 5% have complex tone patterns, and while in some cases this derives from compounding, in others this pattern occurs on monomorphemic words. 1.3 Stress I have not discovered any discussion of stress patterns in Cemuhi.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim in the held cache of Lynch 2002 pp. 753-754. The classification (tonal / TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT, no stress rule, domain UNSTATED) rests on a 2002 handbook sketch that is a faithful abstract of the sole reference grammar (Rivierre 1980), and the tonal verdict is independently corroborated by held material (Lionnet 2022 fn. 9 quoting Rivierre 2001:32 'languages with word tone'; Ferry's 1982 review of Rivierre 1980, fetched sources now: 'possède des tons dont le jeu est très finement décrit'; Wikipedia citing Rivierre 1972/1980). Nothing found on the web (no JIPA illustration, no dissertation, no post-Rivierre Cemuhi prosody study; Lionnet's 2022/2023/2025 accent-and-tone work is on Paici/Xaracuu/Drubea-Numee) suggests a stress system that would change the coding. The weakness is only that the stress line is Lynch's second-hand 'no discussion found' rather than Rivierre's ow

sources.note: The first assessment listed this as library-print-only; it is open on archive.org and was already held under the nemi1240 audit dir. p. 429 + fn. 9 is the only primary statement on Cemuhi accentual properties: tone language with poor tonal morphology, no 'couplage', but demarcative traits (lexeme tone realised preferentially on the initial syllable; final-syllable neutralisations) — the note the record's prule/caution should carry.
